events.ai_basis: v2: 'Agent (D) proved the correctness of the proposed algorithm under an additional type condition on the bipartite graph.' v1: 'For one of these variants, our agent produced a complete proof.'

why: The statement names two conjectures, so even a full proof of the undirected conjecture would be a case; the digraph part has no event. The two claimed full proofs (Mehendale, O'Shea-Wilkins) both predate the snapshot and carry several F10 signals together (landmark claim, years of silence, later specialist sources still calling it open, marginal venue/listing), so they are set aside. The DeepMind bipartite result changes the deck itself (fixed-bipartition bipartite deck, bipartite isomorphism) and adds strong hypotheses, so it is a variant rather than a restriction of the standard conjecture to bipartite graphs; its AI role is generated since the agent produced the proof, but the variant scope discards it. Hartman et al. reconstruct from graphlet degree distributions, which the record says are richer than the deck, so variant. Kostochka et al.'s caterpillar m-deck result adds nothing to the standard conjecture (trees are classically reconstructible), so variant. Interval graphs (Heinrich et al.) and Aravind-Monikandan's reconstructible classes are genuine in-window restrictions of part (a): case. Bérczi's AlphaEvolve work proves nothing by its own statement: none. Calle-Gould is about edge reconstruction: variant.
doubts: O'Shea-Wilkins could not be read and its corrigendum is unknown; if the proof were sound it would still only be a pre-snapshot case. Whether Hartman et al.'s graphlet data are deck-derivable was not established; if they are, some of its classes would be cases. Aravind-Monikandan was read only at abstract level.
